title: The First Physician
tagline: More than four thousand years ago, one man received the world's first doctor's title.

scenes.text: Memphis, Egypt, c. 2700 BCE. The court of Pharaoh Djoser — the same pharaoh who employs Imhotep. Among the officials and scribes, one man holds titles more unusual than any other: Chief of Dentists. Chief of Physicians. His name is carved into the history of medicine forever.

scenes.speaker: Hesy-Ra
scenes.text: The body is a system. Every part connected to every other part. A man comes to me with pain in his jaw — but I must also look at his eyes, his color, his breath. The mouth speaks illness before the patient knows they are ill.

challenge.fact: Hesy-Ra (c. 2700–2600 BCE) is the earliest known physician in recorded history. He held the title 'Chief of Dentists and Physicians' — inscribed on a wooden panel in his tomb at Saqqara, making him the first named doctor in history.
challenge.instruction: Hesy-Ra is considered the first person in history to hold what title? Gather what the story needs: match the goods until the tally is met.

scenes.text: Hesy-Ra is the first physician in recorded history whose name we know. His mastaba tomb at Saqqara contains eleven carved wooden panels — among the greatest artworks of the Old Kingdom. He is depicted carrying scribal tools and physician's instruments, a man whose identity fused art and healing.

scenes.speaker: Royal Patient
scenes.text: Hesy-Ra, the Pharaoh asks — can you ease the toothache that plagues him? He has been awake three nights.

challenge.fact: Hesy-Ra was Chief of Dentists and Physicians under Pharaoh Djoser (c. 2650 BCE). The Step Pyramid at Saqqara, designed by Imhotep, was built during the same reign — making Hesy-Ra and Imhotep contemporaries at the world's most ambitious construction project.
challenge.instruction: Hesy-Ra served under Pharaoh Djoser, who built Egypt's first pyramid at Saqqara. Learn the phrase and play it back, note for note.

scenes.speaker: Hesy-Ra
scenes.text: Bring me oil of juniper, fresh honey, and ground malachite. We will pack the cavity and seal it. But tell the Pharaoh — a tooth this far gone will not last the year. The body forgives much, but it does not forgive being ignored.

challenge.fact: Ancient Egyptian medical knowledge was remarkably advanced. The Edwin Smith Papyrus describes 48 surgical cases with diagnoses, treatments, and prognoses — a clinical approach that would not be surpassed in Europe for thousands of years.

scenes.text: Ancient Egyptian medicine was a sophisticated blend of practical observation and ritual protection. Physicians like Hesy-Ra used herbal compounds, surgical instruments, and anatomical knowledge that would not be surpassed in Europe for two thousand years. The Edwin Smith Papyrus — written centuries later — preserves the tradition he helped establish.

challenge.instruction: Hesy-Ra and Imhotep were contemporaries under Pharaoh Djoser. Fill in the crossword of their shared world — pyramids, medicine, and ancient Egypt.
challenge.fact: Hesy-Ra and Imhotep both served under Djoser at Saqqara around 2650 BCE — one built the world's first pyramid, the other held the world's first physician title. They may have walked the same palace corridors.

scenes.speaker: Hesy-Ra
scenes.text: Carve my name here on this panel. Not as a boast — as a record. Future healers must know this art was practiced. Every physician who comes after me stands on the work of someone who came before. Let them know we were here.

challenge.instruction: Egyptian doctors worked beside priests in the labyrinthine temples of Memphis. Navigate the inner passages — every turn holds a medical secret.
challenge.fact: Egyptian medicine was practised in temple 'Houses of Life' — scriptorium-hospitals where physicians copied medical papyri alongside religious texts. Hesy-Ra's work as both scribe and physician reflects this union of healing and sacred knowledge.
